result:
The afternoon light slanted through the kitchen window, turning dust motes into slow-moving constellations. I stood at the counter with a half-peeled orange, its scent sharp and bright, and listened to the refrigerator’s low hum. Outside, a neighbor’s wind chime answered a breeze I couldn’t feel. Nothing urgent demanded attention, so I let the moment stretch.

I thought about how often we treat time as a resource to be optimized, sliced into tasks and notifications. Yet the orange peel came away in one long spiral, and the simple success of that felt oddly satisfying. The juice ran over my fingers; I didn’t rush to wash them. Instead I watched a single drop fall and spread on the cutting board, darkening the wood grain in a perfect circle.

Memory arrived without invitation: my grandmother’s hands doing the same thing decades ago, her voice explaining that the white pith was bitter but the oil in the skin was worth saving for cakes. I had forgotten the cakes and remembered only the gesture. Now the gesture returned, precise and kind.

When the orange was gone I rinsed my hands and stepped onto the small balcony. The city noise rose and fell like weather. A bus sighed at the corner; somewhere a dog barked twice and stopped. I stayed until the light shifted from gold to amber, noticing how the railing’s shadow lengthened across the floor. No insight arrived, no resolution. Only the quiet knowledge that an ordinary interval, fully inhabited, can hold more than it appears to. I went back inside, the scent of citrus still on my skin, and began to write.
